title: Soap, Then Baking Powder, Then Gum: Wrigley's First Year in Chicago
dek: Arriving in Chicago in 1891 to sell soap, William Wrigley Jr. twice found customers wanted his free gift more than his product, and followed them.

story.event: Dropping soap and then baking powder for the chewing gum he had been giving away
story.summary: William Wrigley Jr. came to Chicago in spring 1891 to sell his father's scouring soap, with $32 by his own account. Merchants resisted until he raised the price and added premiums; selling on his own, he found the baking powder he gave away more popular than the soap, switched to baking powder with chewing gum as the premium, and in 1892, when the gum proved more popular again, concentrated on gum.
paragraphs: In the spring of 1891 William Wrigley Jr., then 29, came to Chicago from Philadelphia to sell his father's scouring soap. By his own account he arrived "with thirty-two dollars and my experience" and rented desk room in an office on East Kinzie Street; two reference histories add a $5,000 loan from an uncle, on condition that a cousin became his partner. The experience was real. He had stirred soap vats in his father's factory and had sold soap on the road since he was thirteen.

Chicago merchants were not keen. At five cents a box, one company history says, the soap left them almost no margin. "It was hard going for a while," Wrigley recalled in 1922. His answer was to raise the retail price to ten cents, giving the grocer a bigger cut, and to add a free umbrella with every box. It worked, he said. For the rest of his working life he argued for giving customers something extra with each purchase.

Striking out on his own, he offered baking powder as the free gift. Customers wanted the gift more than the soap, so by 1892 he had turned to selling baking powder, and needed a new premium. He chose chewing gum, two packets with every can, made for him by an outside firm. For the second time in about a year the extra outsold the product. "The gum became more popular than the baking powder, so I dropped the latter and concentrated my attention on the gum," he said. His first gums, Lotta and Vassar, went on sale in 1892; Juicy Fruit and Spearmint followed.

Concentrating did not make it easy. He gave scales to grocers who ordered fifteen dollars' worth of gum. In 1902 he spent $100,000 advertising in New York and, he said, "hardly made a ripple"; a second $100,000 went the same way before a third, larger campaign won the losses back. Premiums, he admitted, had both made and lost him many thousands of dollars, because "a fellow can't always guess right." By 1922 his factories in four cities were turning out nearly ten billion sticks a year.

quote.text: for obstinacy, from which Fortune often wrings some concession, must needs be anxious and unhappy, but caprice, which can never restrain itself, must be more so.
quote.work: Of Peace of Mind (De Tranquillitate Animi), in the Minor Dialogues
quote.source_title: Minor Dialogues, Together With the Dialogue on Clemency, tr. Aubrey Stewart, Project Gutenberg eBook #64576
quote.connection: Seneca warns against two opposite faults: the obstinacy that will not yield and the caprice that cannot settle. Wrigley dropped soap and then baking powder within about a year, then stayed with gum for life. Whether those first switches were judgement or restlessness, his own account does not say.

reflection: Wrigley did not set out to sell chewing gum. He set out to sell soap, and twice he noticed that what people reached for was the thing he was giving away. Seneca would ask whether that was judgement or restlessness, and the record does not settle it; it shows only that once he found the gum, he stayed.

You may have something like it: a thing people keep coming back to you for that you treat as a side offering, such as the quick explanation, the template, the half-hour you give freely. It might be a signal, or only a pleasant distraction. Watching it for a while before deciding is not indecision.
invitation: Write down one thing people keep asking you for that you treat as extra. Ask one colleague today why it matters to them, and simply listen to the answer.

cross_checks.claim: Wrigley came to Chicago in 1891 with $32.
Merchants resisted the soap until he raised the retail price and added premiums such as umbrellas.
Baking powder given as a premium outsold the soap; gum given with the baking powder then outsold the baking powder, and he concentrated on gum.
His first gum brands, Lotta and Vassar, appeared in 1892.
Early large advertising campaigns failed before later ones paid.

research_notes: Starting capital: in his 1922 Illustrated World interview Wrigley says he came to Chicago with thirty-two dollars and his experience; the Encyclopedia of World Biography and EBSCO's Research Starter add a $5,000 loan from an uncle (EBSCO names him William Scotchard) on condition that his cousin became a partner. Both are given, the loan attributed to the reference histories. Funding is left as 'bootstrapped' since the only outside money was a family loan. Sequence and dates: the International Directory of Company Histories says he dropped soap in 1892 to sell baking powder and then looked for a new premium; its own summary and the Encyclopedia of World Biography put the first gums (Lotta, Vassar) in 1892. Juicy Fruit and Spearmint are dated 1893 by IDCH and Penn State, 1893 and 1894 respectively by EBSCO and EWB, so the story gives no date. Manufacturer: IDCH names Zeno Manufacturing and a 1909 buyout; EBSCO and EWB name the 'Zero' company and 1911; the story says only 'an outside firm'. IDCH says the soap was doubled in price; Wrigley says ten cents a cake (it had been five cents a box per IDCH); IDCH's figure of 65,000 red umbrellas whose dye ran is not used. 1907 advertising figures disagree widely (Wrigley: $3 million in contracts; IDCH: $250,000 borrowed buying $1.5 million of space; EWB and EBSCO: $284,000 spent), so the story leaves 1907 out. IDCH also credits Wrigley with suggesting chicle to Zeno, which other sources do not support; not used. The line 'Everybody likes something extra, for nothing' appears in EWB as something he 'often said' without a date or source, so it is paraphrased, not quoted. The 1922 article is cited from a transcription on todayinsci.com that gives the volume and page numbers. The Seneca sentence comes from a passage on accepting changes of purpose without falling into caprice; the excerpt begins mid-sentence.
